header.title_plain: A 60–90 s all-out cycling test gave the same anaerobic-capacity estimate (accumulated oxygen deficit) as riding to exhaustion at a fixed supramaximal workload.

citation.title: Accumulated oxygen deficit during supramaximal all-out and constant intensity exercise
citation.authors: Gastin PB, Costill DL, Lawson DL, Krzeminski K, McConell GK
citation.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise

header.evidence_type: Two separate method-comparison studies with no training period. Study 1: 9 active men, three supramaximal cycle tests (constant ~110% and ~125% VO2max to exhaustion, and an isokinetic all-out test) in random order. Study 2: 12 subjects (6 untrained, 6 endurance trained; sex not stated), a constant ~110% VO2max test to exhaustion and a 90 s all-out test; order not stated as randomised. No blinding stated. Each test performed once per subject.

confidence.why: The hand entry rated this preliminary–moderate; preliminary is chosen because each study is small (n = 9 and n = 12), each test was done once with no test–retest reliability data, AOD is an indirect estimate built on an extrapolated oxygen cost, and 'not significantly different' was not backed by an equivalence test, although the result did replicate across two labs and two ergometers.

practical_relevance.why: A method-validation paper for lab testing; the single practical point is that a 60–90 s all-out effort captures anaerobic capacity about as well as a constant-pace ride to exhaustion, which matters to whoever designs tests rather than to day-to-day programming.

header.author_stance: The study 2 all-out protocol is a modification of a variable-resistance test previously published by the first author's group (Gastin et al., ref 14), so the authors are validating a protocol from their own lab; no other interest is apparent.

comparison.design_notes: Two independent studies run by the first author in separate labs. Before the supramaximal tests, each subject did a VO2max test and a series of submaximal rides (study 1: six to eight 7 min rides from 80 W rising 40 W per ride, 29 ± 2 to 84 ± 2% VO2max, 80–360 W; study 2: five to six 5 min rides at 46 ± 1 to 81 ± 2% VO2max, steady state accepted when VO2 changed by less than 0.6 ml·kg−1 (<50 ml) from the 4th to 5th min). The linear oxygen-cost-versus-power relationship was extrapolated to estimate the oxygen cost of each supramaximal test (Medbø method); AOD = estimated oxygen cost minus measured oxygen uptake. Tests 2–7 d apart at the same time of day, after 24 h of standardised diet and limited activity and at least 4 h fasting. Study 1 used Douglas bags; study 2 breath-by-breath. Study 1 fibre type from a vastus lateralis biopsy (ATPase stain, ~400 fibres). Statistics: study 1 one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Newman-Keuls post hoc; study 2 two-tailed paired t-test; P < 0.05; data mean ± SEM. Peak blood lactate was not reported for study 2. The authors note AOD variance may be higher than other measures because it is derived from several measures each with its own variance, and that AOD may not be a valid measure of anaerobic capacity at all (with references). No invasive validation of AOD was done. No test–retest reliability data, no equivalence test.

layer2.what_it_means: Across two separate studies, the estimated anaerobic capacity (accumulated oxygen deficit, AOD) came out the same whether riders went all-out or held a fixed supramaximal workload until exhaustion: 43.9, 44.1 and 42.0 ml·kg−1 for the three study-1 tests and 52.1 versus 51.2 ml·kg−1 in study 2. The calculated anaerobic work was also unchanged across tests (208–215 J·kg−1 in study 1, 249 J·kg−1 for both study-2 tests), while total and aerobic work grew with test length: the 110% rides lasted 186–208 s and drew 74–76% of their energy aerobically, against 51–57% for the 62–90 s all-out tests. The practical reading is that a 60–90 s all-out effort exhausts the anaerobic reserve about as fully as a constant-pace ride to failure, while also yielding peak power, mean power and a fatigue index from the same test. It also shows why total work in a long sprint test partly reflects aerobic fitness rather than anaerobic capacity alone. Individual results were less consistent than the averages: a rider's AOD differed between tests by 4.0 ml·kg−1 on average in study 1 and 4.7 ml·kg−1 in study 2, with differences up to 13.2 ml·kg−1.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: This does not show the two test types are interchangeable for an individual. The comparison found no significant difference; no equivalence test was run, and individual differences reached 10.3 and 13.2 ml·kg−1. In study 2, untrained subjects tended to score higher on the all-out test and endurance-trained subjects on the constant test, though each subgroup had only six people. Samples were small (9 and 12), study 1 was young active men, study 2's sex is not stated, and nobody was older, female by report, or a trained sprinter. Each test was performed once, so day-to-day reliability is unknown. AOD is an indirect estimate: it depends on extrapolating oxygen cost from submaximal rides, assumes efficiency holds above VO2max, and the authors themselves cite work questioning whether AOD validly measures anaerobic capacity. Results apply to seated cycling on two specific lab ergometers, not to running, rowing or field tests, and the paper says nothing about training anaerobic capacity.

translation: A 60–90 s all-out bike test gave an anaerobic-capacity estimate not significantly different from riding to failure at about 110–125% of VO2max (42.0 vs 43.9–44.1 ml/kg in one study, 51.2 vs 52.1 ml/kg in the other).
Riding to failure at about 110% lasted 186–208 s and did more total work (921–979 vs 429–576 J/kg), but anaerobic work did not differ; the extra was aerobic.

glossary_candidates.definition: The gap between the oxygen a hard effort would need and the oxygen actually used, added up over the effort. Used as an estimate of how much energy came from anaerobic sources.
Work at an intensity above the power that produces VO2max, so it cannot be supplied by aerobic metabolism alone and can only be held briefly.
The total amount of energy a person can produce without oxygen (from phosphocreatine and glycolysis) before that supply is used up.
A test in which the workload is fixed in advance and the rider holds it until they can no longer keep the required cadence.
A test in which the athlete goes as hard as possible from the start for a set time or until power drops below a cut-off, so power is high early and fades.
An exercise machine that holds cadence at a fixed speed (here 90 rpm) however hard the rider pushes, so only the force and power change.
A standard 30 s all-out cycling test against a fixed resistance set from body weight, used to measure peak and mean anaerobic power.
How much power falls during an all-out test, from the peak to the minimum, expressed as a percentage of the peak.
The highest lactate concentration measured in blood after a hard effort; a rough marker of how much glycolysis was used.
The highest rate at which a person can take up and use oxygen during exercise, usually in ml per kg body weight per minute.
A straight line linking power output to oxygen use, built from several easier rides and extended upward to estimate the oxygen a supramaximal effort would need.
A measure of how precisely a group average is known; it is smaller than the spread between individuals, so ± SEM values look tighter than the real person-to-person variation.
A number from −1 to 1 describing how closely two measures rise or fall together; 0 means no straight-line relationship.
The share of fast-twitch fibres in a small muscle sample removed with a needle, here from the outer thigh (vastus lateralis).
Two ways to measure oxygen uptake: collecting expired air in large bags for analysis, or analysing each breath continuously with a metabolic cart.
